records.claim: Fermentation temperature influences yeast activity and fermentation speed; within a strain's workable range, warmer conditions generally increase yeast activity and can shorten fermentation time.
records.notes: General direction only; exact fermentation behavior remains strain- and process-dependent.

records.claim: Fermentation temperature can change yeast-derived flavor and aroma, but the size and direction of that change are strain-dependent; a warmer fermentation does not produce the same flavor response in every yeast strain.
records.notes: Avoid teaching temperature-to-flavor effects as universal absolutes; source material documents strain-specific exceptions.

records.claim: Fermentation temperature targets should be chosen with strain-specific guidance rather than treated as one universal ale or lager temperature rule.
records.notes: Practical course guidance derived from multiple manufacturer technical sources; the registry classification remains professional_interpretation, separate from verification status.

records.claim: During mashing, malt enzymes -- primarily alpha- and beta-amylase -- break down starch; not all of it is broken all the way down into fermentable sugars, and some is instead converted into larger dextrins that ordinary brewing yeast does not ferment.

sources.ref: Briess Technical Services (Bies, D. & Roberts, C., 2013), 'Understanding a Malt Analysis'
The Oxford Companion to Beer (Garrett Oliver, ed., 2011), entry 'alpha amylase'

records.notes: Alpha- and beta-amylase act together during mashing; their relative activity, not just overall enzyme presence, determines how much starch converts to fermentable sugar versus unfermentable dextrin.

records.claim: In a study that varied mash temperature between 65C and 80C, increasing mash temperature within that range reduced the fermentability of the resulting wort; mash thickness also affected the outcome.

sources.ref: R. Muller (1991), 'The effects of mashing temperature and mash thickness on wort carbohydrate composition', Journal of the Institute of Brewing 97(2):85-92, DOI 10.1002/j.2050-0416.1991.tb01055.x

records.notes: Only the abstract/metadata of this source were directly verified in this round; the publisher's full text was not accessible (returned HTTP 403). The claim is deliberately scoped to the exact 65-80C range and the temperature/thickness effects the abstract itself reports -- it must not be read as generic beginner mash-temperature guidance (80C is well above a typical beginner saccharification target) without a separate source that supports that broader, practical-brewing claim.

records.claim: The iodine test checks mash or wort for residual starch: a drop of iodine solution turning blue-black indicates starch is still present, while no blue-black color change indicates the starch has been converted.

sources.ref: The Oxford Companion to Beer (Garrett Oliver, ed., 2011), entry 'iodine'

records.notes: Not promoted to 'verified' in this round: issue #337 requires an independent second suitable source for this specific claim before promotion, and only one source (The Oxford Companion to Beer, entry 'iodine') was available/verifiable in this round. Promote only after a second independent source is found and reviewed. Not referenced by the shipped mashing.fundamentals pilot content for this reason.

records.claim: Mash temperature is only one of several factors -- including mash thickness/water-to-grist ratio and the malt's own enzyme content -- that influence wort fermentability and carbohydrate composition; there is no single mash temperature that is universally correct for every recipe or desired beer outcome.

sources.ref: R. Muller (1991), 'The effects of mashing temperature and mash thickness on wort carbohydrate composition', Journal of the Institute of Brewing 97(2):85-92, DOI 10.1002/j.2050-0416.1991.tb01055.x
Briess Technical Services (Bies, D. & Roberts, C., 2013), 'Understanding a Malt Analysis'

records.notes: Practical course guidance synthesized from multiple sources; the registry classification remains professional_interpretation, separate from verification status, mirroring FACT-BREW-0003's precedent.

records.claim: Boiling wort to an active, sustained boil inactivates the malt enzymes that were active during mashing (stopping further starch conversion) and reduces the wort's microbial load carried over from the mash/lauter.

sources.type: established brewing-science technical text (Kunze, Technology Brewing and Malting, cited in a Brewers Association-hosted VLB presentation)

records.notes: Scope: 'reduces microbial load at the time of boiling', not a claim that the wort/kettle/equipment remains sterile afterward -- post-boil handling (chilling, transfer, fermenter sanitation) can still introduce contamination. No specific minimum time/temperature threshold is asserted. Wording trap: never say 'sterilizes'; never attach a specific minute count as a universal rule.

records.claim: Barley/malt contains a precursor that can form dimethyl sulfide (DMS) during wort heating; DMS itself is volatile, and a vigorous, sufficiently long boil is one important control that helps prevent DMS off-flavor in finished beer.

sources.type: Brewers Association off-flavor management resource covering DMS

records.notes: The precursor and DMS are distinct; this claim does not require the learner to identify or quantify the precursor. No universal minimum boil duration or malt-type threshold is asserted -- precursor levels vary by malt (more relevant for base malts like pilsner malt). Critical wording trap (issue #366 guardrail): never call the precursor itself 'volatile' or 'the thing driven off' -- DMS is what is volatile and driven off, the precursor is what forms it. Do not state a fixed 'X minutes removes all DMS risk' rule.

records.claim: Boiling causes wort proteins and polyphenols to coagulate and precipitate out -- the 'hot break'.

sources.type: established brewing-science technical text (Kunze, Technology Brewing and Malting, cited in a Brewers Association-hosted VLB presentation)

records.notes: Narrowed to the coagulation/precipitation phenomenon itself -- does not assert a specific haze/off-flavor/staling benefit from removing that material. Explicitly distinct from chill haze, which forms later, on cooling, from a different (colder-temperature) protein-polyphenol interaction. Wording trap: never conflate 'hot break' and 'chill haze' as the same phenomenon.

records.claim: In the first minutes after a wort reaches a rolling boil, a rising foam commonly forms and can rise fast enough to boil over the kettle if the kettle is fairly full and the brewer is not watching; briefly reducing heat, using an anti-foam aid, or staying attentive during this window is common homebrewing practice to prevent it.

sources.type: established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 7)

records.notes: An established, widely observed brewing practice, not a controlled study result -- does not claim a boil-over always happens, nor quantify a fill-level threshold. Wording trap: do not present as a guaranteed event ('will boil over'); do not imply a single fixed fill percentage is safe for every kettle geometry.

records.claim: Boiling converts (isomerizes) hop alpha acids into the more soluble iso-alpha-acids that are a major source of perceived bitterness in beer. Isomerization is time-dependent: a longer boil time for a given addition increases its bitterness contribution (utilization), but utilization approaches a practical ceiling rather than increasing without bound as boil time grows.

sources.type: peer-reviewed experimental review of hop alpha-acid isomerisation/utilisation

records.notes: Describes the direction and the general isomerization/utilization relationship only -- does not assert alpha acids contribute zero bitterness before isomerization, and does not assert or reproduce any specific numeric utilization curve or percentage (that remains modules/calculations.py's own implemented Tinseth model, out of scope for this teaching claim). Wording trap: do not say alpha acids are 'not bitter' before isomerization; do not state a specific utilization percentage or claim any one utilization model is the single, universally accepted number.

records.claim: Hop aroma and flavor come largely from volatile essential oils, which boil off the longer a hop addition remains in an active boil. An addition made late in the boil, at flameout, or during a post-boil whirlpool/hop-stand therefore generally retains more of its original aroma/flavor character, and generally reaches lower alpha-acid utilization (bitterness), than an otherwise-comparable early/full-boil addition -- though a hot, long whirlpool/hop-stand can still contribute material bitterness, not zero.

sources.type: AHA technical experiment with Bell's Brewery lab IBU measurements

records.notes: 'Generally lower' utilization, not 'zero' or 'negligible' -- a hot, long whirlpool/hop-stand can still contribute material bitterness. Does not assert an exact cutoff or any particular whirlpool temperature/duration as optimal. Wording trap: never say a late/whirlpool addition contributes 'zero' or 'negligible' bitterness; do not assert one specific 'correct' whirlpool temperature or hold time as a universal rule.

records.claim: Because bitterness contribution (favored by longer boil time, FACT-HOP-0001) and aroma/flavor retention (favored by shorter boil time, FACT-HOP-0002) move in opposite directions with boil time, brewers commonly use hop additions at more than one point in the process -- e.g. an early 'bittering' addition plus a late or whirlpool 'aroma/flavor' addition -- to pursue both independently in the same beer, rather than relying on a single addition.

sources.type: peer-reviewed experimental review of hop alpha-acid isomerisation/utilisation
AHA technical experiment with Bell's Brewery lab IBU measurements

records.notes: A synthesis/interpretation of FACT-HOP-0001/FACT-HOP-0002, not a new independently measured result -- describes a common brewing strategy, not a fixed numeric schedule (does not assert e.g. '60/20/5 minutes' as a required recipe). No independent citation beyond the two underlying facts' own sources is expected, mirroring FACT-MASH-0004's precedent. Wording trap: do not present any specific minute schedule as the correct or only pattern; do not imply single-addition recipes are wrong.
